definition: To claim or take a power, right, or privilege for yourself without having any right to it.
example: The new office manager tried to arrogate to himself the right to approve every purchase in the building.
nuance: Arrogate means grabbing a right you were never given. It is often confused with abrogate, which means to formally cancel a law or agreement.
prompt: A club treasurer starts making decisions that are supposed to belong to the whole board.
options: The treasurer began to arrogate the power to cancel events without asking the board.
The board voted to arrogate the outdated rule about where meetings must be held.
Feeling overwhelmed, the treasurer decided to arrogate her authority and hand every decision back to the board.
After a fair vote, the members asked her to arrogate the budget duties for one more year.
reasons: She is taking an authority that was never hers, which is exactly what this verb describes.
Formally repealing a rule is abrogating it. This mixes up two look-alike words.
Giving power away is the reverse of claiming it, so relinquish would fit here.
Duties granted by a fair vote are not taken without right, so the word's negative sense is lost.

practice.prompt: Four students are presenting a science project they built together.
options: Generous to a fault, Malik offered to arrogate his share of the credit so his teammates would receive more praise.
Malik was pleased to arrogate the bonus points the teacher had fairly awarded to him.
Without asking anyone, Malik tried to arrogate all the credit for the group's results.
Malik began to arrogate his teammates about where they had found their data.
reasons: Giving up credit is the opposite of grabbing it.
Accepting points he earned fairly involves no unjust claim, so the verb does not fit.
Claiming shared credit for himself alone is taking something he has no right to.
Questioning people closely is interrogating them. This confuses the word with a similar-sounding one.
